strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a practical clinical NLP bottleneck: access to annotated clinical text. Its 8,767 synthetic examples, broad category coverage, span annotations, temporal attributes, and rationales constitute a useful resource contribution.

Real-data experiments support the dataset’s utility for smaller models. Prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F on MIMIC-SBDH, while standard RoBERTa improves from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH. These results demonstrate benefits beyond evaluation on synthetic text alone.

Expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples, including correction, addition, deletion, and adjudication of annotations, provides a valuable evaluation resource. Category-level error analysis and training-size experiments help characterize where the dataset succeeds and fails.

The generation prompts, 45 seed examples, annotation guidelines, training configurations, and three-run results provide substantial methodological documentation. Together with the reported dataset and checkpoint release, the supported resource and augmentation contribution warrant Findings.
weaknesses: The claim of consistent improvement is broader than the results support. VA-SBDH NER gains are small or absent for encoder models, and Llama models obtain essentially no benefit. The dramatic T5 improvement partly reflects an unstable baseline (25.44 ± 18.24 macro-F). The largest category-level gain concerns only 18 positive test examples; variation across training seeds does not capture uncertainty from this small evaluation sample.

Comparative evidence is incomplete. Appendix D.2 claims superiority over MIMIC-SBDH pretraining, but Table 13 does not separately identify results for that condition. Comparisons with class weighting, rare-class oversampling, or additional target-data training would help establish the dataset’s advantages beyond addressing imbalance and providing extra task training.

Generalization is demonstrated within a limited setting: models receive labeled target-domain fine-tuning, the public real-data evaluation covers four aligned categories, and real-data NER relies on restricted VA-SBDH. Synthetic examples average 13.7 words versus 35–47 words in the real datasets, and the seeds reflect VHA experience. These experiments support supervised adaptation but provide limited evidence for transfer to unseen institutions or broader clinical writing styles.

The rationale-distillation claim is weakly supported. Table 5 shows only 0.66 and 0.58 absolute macro-F improvements, with the latter nonsignificant (p=0.36), exclusively on synthetic test text. This does not establish transfer of reasoning capability to real clinical data. Temporal prediction and explicit negation extraction are also not directly evaluated despite being highlighted dataset features.

Annotation-quality claims require careful qualification. Experts added 581 annotations, updated 286, and discarded 142, while training labels remain uncorrected. The 71.06% alignment statistic includes added annotations in its denominator and uses relaxed span matching; it is not ordinary exact-match annotation accuracy. Reviewers also saw GPT-4 suggestions, limiting independence. Reporting agreement separately for spans, categories, presence, and temporality would make the quality assessment more interpretable.

Some reporting details impede reproducibility: the significance-testing procedure is insufficiently specified, and the ROUGE-L filtering description says an example must resemble all previous examples to be excluded. Clarifying whether this means any previous example is necessary because the two rules produce substantially different datasets.
